And the warning is not at variance with the fact that, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.9">1Sa 6:9</reference>, the priests still entertained some doubt whether the plagues really did come from Jehovah at all: for their doubts did not preclude the possibility of its being so; and even the possibility might be sufficient to make it seem advisable to do everything that could be done to mitigate the wrath of the God of the Israelites, of whom, under existing circumstances, the heathen stood not only no less, but even more, in dread, than of the wrath of their own gods.
entries.daa624b04fea71cea639c494fdc0b8b793ad14ce: <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.7-1Sam.6.9">1Sa 6:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen3735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3736" type="x-p"/> Accordingly they arranged the sending back in such a manner as to manifest the reverence which ought to be shown to the God of Israel was a powerful deity (<reference osisRef="1Sam.6.7-1Sam.6.9">1Sa 6:7-9</reference>). The Philistines were to take a new cart and make it ready (עשׂה), and to yoke two milch cows to the cart upon which no yoke had ever come, and to take away their young ones (calves) from them into the house, i.e., into the stall, and then to put the ark upon the cart, along with the golden things to be presented as a trespass-offering, which were to be in a small chest by the side of the ark, and to send it (i.e., the ark) away, that it might go, viz., without the cows being either driven or guided. From the result of these arrangements, they were to learn whether the plague had been sent by the God of Israel, or had arisen accidentally. “<hi type="italic">If it</hi> (the ark) <hi type="italic">goeth up by the way to its border towards Bethshemesh, He</hi> (Jehovah) <hi type="italic">hath done us this great evil; but if not, we perceive that His hand hath not touched us. It came to us by chance</hi>,” i.e., the evil came upon us merely by accident. In עליהם, בּניהם, and מאחריהם (<reference osisRef="1Sam.6.7">1Sa 6:7</reference>), the masculine is used in the place of the more definite feminine, as being the more general form. This is frequently the case, and occurs again in <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.10">1Sa 6:10</reference> and 1Sa 6:12. ארגּז, which only occurs again in <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.8">1Sa 6:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.11">1Sa 6:11</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.15">1Sa 6:15</reference>, signifies, according to the context and the ancient versions, a chest or little case. The suffix to אתו refers to the ark, which is also the subject to יעלה (<reference osisRef="1Sam.6.9">1Sa 6:9</reference>). גּבוּלו, the territory of the ark, is the land of Israel, where it had its home. מקרה is used adverbially: by chance, or accidentally. The new cart and the young cows, which had never worn a yoke, corresponded to the holiness of the ark of God. To place it upon an old cart, which had already been used for all kinds of earthly purposes, would have been an offence against the holy thing; and it would have been just the same to yoke to the cart animals that had already been used for drawing, and had had their strength impaired by the yoke (see <reference osisRef="Deut.21.3">Deu 21:3</reference>). The reason for selecting cows, however, instead of male oxen, was no doubt to be found in the further object which they hoped to attain. It was certainly to be expected, that if suckling cows, whose calves had been kept back from them, followed their own instincts, without any drivers, they would not go away, but would come back to their young ones in the stall. And if the very opposite should take place, this would be a sure sign that they were driven and guided by a divine power, and in fact by the God whose ark they were to draw into His own land. From this they would be able to draw the conclusion, that the plagues which had fallen upon the Philistines were also sent by this God. There was no special sagacity in this advice of the priests; it was nothing more than a cleverly devised attempt to put the power of the God of the Israelites to the text, though they thereby unconsciously and against their will furnished the occasion for the living God to display His divine glory before those who did not know Him.
entries.01ae559d54b8b7a71e444f24d2f1f2f51e173c22: <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.10-1Sam.6.12">1Sa 6:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen3736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3737" type="x-p"/> The God of Israel actually did what the idolatrous priests hardly considered possible. When the Philistines, in accordance with the advice given them by their priests, had placed the ark of the covenant and the expiatory gifts upon the cart to which the two cows were harnessed, “<hi type="italic">the cows went straight forward on the way to Bethshemesh; they went along a road going and lowing</hi> (i.e., lowing the whole time), <hi type="italic">and turned not to the right or to the left; and the princes of the Philistines went behind them to the territory of Bethshemesh</hi>.” בּדּרך ישּׁרנה, lit., “<hi type="italic">they were straight in the way</hi>,” i.e., they went straight along the road. The form ישּׁרנה for יישׁרנה is the imperf. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, third pers. plur. fem., with the preformative י instead of ת, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.30.38">Gen 30:38</reference> (see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §47, Anm. 3; <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §191, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). <hi type="italic">Bethshemesh</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Ain-shems</hi>, was a priests’ city on the border of Judah and Dan (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.10">Jos 15:10</reference>).
entries.713429dae7ee99858e800763b11a4bdf887416ce: <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.13-1Sam.6.14">1Sa 6:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen3737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3738" type="x-p"/> The inhabitants of Bethshemesh were busy with the wheat-harvest in the valley (in front of the town), when they unexpectedly saw the ark of the covenant coming, and rejoiced to see it. The cart had arrived at the field of Joshua, a Bethshemeshite, and there it stood still before a large stone. And they (the inhabitants of Bethshemesh) chopped up the wood of the cart, and offered the cows to the Lord as a burnt-offering. In the meantime the Levites had taken off the ark, with the chest of golden presents, and placed it upon the large stone; and the people of Bethshemesh offered burnt-offerings and slain-offerings that day to the Lord. The princes of the Philistines stood looking at this, and then returned the same day to Ekron. That the Bethshemeshites, and not the Philistines, are the subject to ויבקּעוּ, is evident from the correct interpretation of the clauses; viz., from the fact that in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Sam.6.14">1Sa 6:14</reference></hi> the words from והעגלה to גּדולה אבן are circumstantial clauses introduced into the main clause, and that ויבקּעוּ is attached to לראות ויּשׂמחוּ, and carries on the principal clause.
entries.e9daf250f130800b6b92acf048f0ceec3176c1a9: <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.15-1Sam.6.18">1Sa 6:15-18</reference> <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Sam.6.15">1Sa 6:15</reference></hi> contains a supplementary remark, therefore הורידוּ is to be translated as a pluperfect. After sacrificing the cart, with the cows, as a burnt-offering to the Lord, the inhabitants of Bethshemesh gave a further practical expression to their joy at the return of the ark, by offering burnt-offerings and slain-offerings in praise of God. In the burnt-offerings they consecrated themselves afresh, with all their members, to the service of the Lord; and in the slain-offerings, which culminated in the sacrificial meals, they sealed anew their living fellowship with the Lord. The offering of these sacrifices at Bethshemesh was no offence against the commandment, to sacrifice to the Lord at the place of His sanctuary alone. The ark of the covenant was the throne of the gracious presence of God, before which the sacrifices were really offered at the tabernacle. The Lord had sanctified the ark afresh as the throne of His presence, by the miracle which He had wrought in bringing it back again. - In <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.17">1Sa 6:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.18">1Sa 6:18</reference> the different atoning presents, which the Philistines sent to Jehovah as compensation, are enumerated once more: viz., five golden boils, one for each of their five principal towns (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>), and “<hi type="italic">golden mice, according to the number of all the Philistian towns of the five princes, from the fortified city to the village of the inhabitants of the level land</hi>” (<hi type="italic">perazi</hi>; see at <reference osisRef="Deut.3.5">Deu 3:5</reference>). The priests had only proposed that five golden mice should be sent as compensation, as well as five boils (<reference osisRef="1Sam.6.4">1Sa 6:4</reference>). But the Philistines offered as many images of mice as there were towns and villages in their five states, no doubt because the plague of mice had spread over the whole land, whereas the plague of boils had only fallen upon the inhabitants of those towns to which the ark of the covenant had come. In this way the apparent discrepancy between <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.4">1Sa 6:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.18">1Sa 6:18</reference> is very simply removed. The words which follow, viz., וגו עליה הגּיחוּ עשׁר, “<hi type="italic">upon which they had set down the ark</hi>,” show unmistakeably, when compared with <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.14">1Sa 6:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.15">1Sa 6:15</reference>, that we are to understand by הגּדולה אבל the great stone upon which the ark was placed when it was taken off the cart. The conjecture of Kimchi, that this stone was called <hi type="italic">Abel</hi> (<hi type="italic">luctus</hi>), on account of the mourning which took place there (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.19">1Sa 6:19</reference>), is extremely unnatural. Consequently there is no other course left than to regard אבל as an error in writing for אבן, according to the reading, or at all events the rendering, adopted by the lxx and <hi type="italic">Targum</hi>. But ועד (even unto) is quite unsuitable here, as no further local definition is required after the foregoing הפּרי כּפר ועד, and it is impossible to suppose that the Philistines offered a golden mouse as a trespass-offering for the great stone upon which the ark was placed. We must therefore alter ועד into ועד: “<hi type="italic">And the great stone is witness</hi> (for ועד in this sense, see <reference osisRef="Gen.31.52">Gen 31:52</reference>) <hi type="italic">to this day in the field of Joshua the Bethshemeshite</hi>,” sc., of the fact just described.
entries.09cb189d818338576ba7b4cd821d3870d9387eb1: <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.19-1Sam.6.21">1Sa 6:19-21</reference> <div eID="gen3738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3739" type="x-p"/> Disposal of the Ark of God. - 1Sa 6:19. As the ark had brought evil upon the Philistines, so the inhabitants of Bethshemesh were also to be taught that they could not stand in their unholiness before the holy God: “<hi type="italic">And He</hi> (God) <hi type="italic">smote among the men of Bethshemesh, because they had looked at the ark of Jehovah, and smote among the people seventy men, fifty thousand men</hi>.” In this statement of numbers we are not only struck by the fact that the 70 stands before the 50,000, which is very unusual, but even more by the omission of the copula ו before the second number, which is altogether unparalleled. When, in addition to this, we notice that 50,000 men could not possibly live either in or round Bethshemesh, and that we cannot conceive of any extraordinary gathering having taken place out of the whole land, or even from the immediate neighbourhood; and also that the words אישׁ אלף חמשּׁים are wanting in several Hebrew MSS, and that Josephus, in his account of the occurrence, only speaks of <hi type="italic">seventy</hi> as having been killed (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. vi. 1, 4); we cannot come to any other conclusion than that the number 50,000 is neither correct nor genuine, but a gloss which has crept into the text through some oversight, though it is of great antiquity, since the number stood in the text employed by the Septuagint and Chaldee translators, who attempted to explain them in two different ways, but both extremely forced. Apart from this number, however, the verse does not contain anything either in form or substance that could furnish occasion for well-founded objections to its integrity. The repetition of ויּך simply resumes the thought that had been broken off by the parenthetical clause יי בּארון ראוּ כּי; and בּעם is only a general expression for שׁ בּאנשׁי ב. The stroke which fell upon the people of Bethshemesh is sufficiently accounted for in the words, “<hi type="italic">because they had looked</hi>,” etc. There is no necessity to understand these words, however, as many Rabbins do, as signifying “they looked <hi type="italic">into</hi> the ark,” i.e., opened it and looked in; for if this had been the meaning, the opening would certainly not have been passed over without notice. ראה with ב means to look <hi type="italic">upon</hi> or <hi type="italic">at</hi> a thing with lust or malicious pleasure; and here it no doubt signifies a foolish staring, which was incompatible with the holiness of the ark of God, and was punished with death, according to the warning expressed in Num 4:20. This severe judgment so alarmed the people of Bethshemesh, that they exclaimed, “<hi type="italic">Who is able to stand before Jehovah, this holy God!</hi>” Consequently the Bethshemeshites discerned correctly enough that the cause of the fatal stroke, which had fallen upon them, was the unholiness of their own nature, and not any special crime which had been committed by the persons slain. They felt that they were none of them any better than those who had fallen, and that sinners could not approach the holy God. Inspired with this feeling, they added, “<hi type="italic">and to whom shall He go away from us?</hi>” The subject to יעלה is not the ark, but Jehovah who had chosen the ark as the dwelling-place of His name. In order to avert still further judgments, they sought to remove the ark from their town. They therefore sent messengers to Kirjath-jearim to announce to the inhabitants the fact that the ark had been sent back by the Philistines, and to entreat them to fetch it away.  <chapter eID="1Sam.6"/> <div eID="gen3739" type="x-p"/>

As for the first, though they might not chuse Females for that use: yet when God himself had chosen, and in a manner Consecrated them to his service, and imployed them in so Sacred and Gloti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous a Work, it may seem tollerable to offer them to the Lord, as being his peculiar, and improper for any other use. And for the latter, we have many instances of Sacrifices offered to God by Prophets, and Holy Men, in other places, besides the Tabernacle, upon extraordinary occasions, such as this certain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly was; it being fit, that the Ark should at its first return be re<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eived with Thanksgiving and Sacrifice; and this Place being Sanctified by the presence of the Ark, which was the very soul of the Tabernacle, and that by which the Taber<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nacle it self was Sanctified, and for whose sake the Sacrifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces were offered at the door of the Tabernacle.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:221" />15 And the Levites took down <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>For the Levites had taken down:</ns0:hi> for this, though mentioned after, was done before the Sacrifices were offe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red.</ns0:note> the ark of the LORD, and the coffer that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> with it, wherein the jewels of gold <ns0:hi>were,</ns0:hi> and put them on the great stone: and the men of Bethshemesh offered burnt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />offerings, and sacrificed sacrifices the same day unto the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And when the five LORDS of the Philistines had seen <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To wit, that prodigious return of the Ark to its own Countrey, and the entertainment it found there.</ns0:note>, they returned to Ekron the same day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And these <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the golden emerods which the Philistines returned <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> a trespass-<ns0:hi>offering</ns0:hi> unto the LORD: for Ashdod one, for Gaza one, for Askelon one, for Gath one, for Ekron one.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And the golden mice <ns0:hi>according</ns0:hi> to the num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber of all the cities of the Philistines, <ns0:hi>belonging</ns0:hi> to the five lords: <ns0:hi>both</ns0:hi> of fenced cities, and of coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trey villages <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This is added for explication of that foregoing Phrase, <ns0:hi>all the cities;</ns0:hi> either to shew, that under the Name of the five Cities were comprehended all the Villages and Territories belonging to them, in whose Name, and at whose Charge these presents were made; or to express the difference between this and the former present, the Emerods being onely five, according to the five Cities mentioned, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17. because it may seem, the Cities onely, or principally, were pestered with that Disease; and the <ns0:hi>Mice</ns0:hi> being many more, according <ns0:hi>to the number of all the Cities,</ns0:hi> as is here expressed: the Word <ns0:hi>city</ns0:hi> being taken generally so, as to include, not onely Fenced Cities, but also the Country Villages, as is here added, and the Fields belonging to them, these being the parts where the <ns0:hi>Mice</ns0:hi> did most mischief.</ns0:note> even unto the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> great stone.</ns0:note> great <ns0:hi>stone of</ns0:hi> Abel <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which is mentioned as the utmost border of the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> Territory to which the Plague of <ns0:hi>Mice</ns0:hi> did extend. The Word <ns0:hi>stone</ns0:hi> being easily understood out of <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. where this <ns0:hi>great stone</ns0:hi> is expresly mentioned, as the place on which the Ark was set, which is also here repeated in the following words. And this place is here called <ns0:hi>Abel,</ns0:hi> by anticipation, from the great Mourning men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned in the following Verse.</ns0:note>, whereon they set down the ark of the LORD, <ns0:hi>which stone remaineth</ns0:hi> unto this day in the field of Joshua the Bethshemite.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 ¶ And he smote the men of Beth-shemesh, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they had looked into the ark of the LORD <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Having now an opportunity which they never yet had, no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> were ever like to have, it is not strange they had a ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hement curiosity and desire to see the contents of the Ark: or whether the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> had taken them away, and put other things in their place; and they thought they might now presume the more, because the Ark had been polluted by the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> and was now exposed to open view, and not yet put into that Most Holy Place, which they were for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bidden to approach.</ns0:note>, even he smote of the people <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of the people living in, and near <ns0:hi>Bethshemesh,</ns0:hi> or coming thither from all parts upon this great and glorious occasion. Heb. <ns0:hi>And,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Also he <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> of the people;</ns0:hi> to wit, of or belonging to other pla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, though now here: So these are distinguished from the <ns0:hi>men of Bethshemesh,</ns0:hi> of whom he speaks onely in general and indefinitely, <ns0:hi>he smote the men; i. e.</ns0:hi> Some, or many of them, and then sets down the number of the persons smitten, or s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>in, either excluding the <ns0:hi>Bethshemites,</ns0:hi> or including them.</ns0:note> fifty thousand and threescore and ten men <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This may seem an incredible Relation, both because that place could not afford so great a number, and because it seems an act of great rigour, that God should so severely punish those people who came with so much Zeal and Joy to Congratulate the return of the Ark, and that for so inconside<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable an Errour. For the latter branch of the Objection, it may be said, 1. That God always used to be most severe in Punishing his own People, as Sinning against more know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge and warning than others; especially, for such sins as immediately concern his own Worship and Service. 2. That men are very incompetent Judges of these Matters, because they do not understand all the reasons and causes of Gods Judgments. For although God took this just occasion to punish them for that Crime which was so severely forbidden even to the common <ns0:hi>Levites</ns0:hi> under pain of Death; of which see <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 4. 18, 19, 20. Yet it is apparent, that the People were at this time guilty of many other, and greater Miscar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riages, for which God might justly inflict the present pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nishment upon them: and moreover, there are many secret Sins which escape Mans Observation, but are seen by God, before whom, many persons may be deeply guilty, whom men esteem innocent and vertuous. And therefore men should take heed of Censuring the Judgments of God, of which it is most truly said, that they are oft secret, but ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver unrighteous. And for the former branch of the Ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jection, many things are, or may be said; 1. That the Land of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> was strangely populous, See 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 24. 9. and 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 3. 2. That all these were not the setled Inha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bitants of this place, but most of them such as did, and in all probability would resort thither in great numbers upon so illustrious an occasion. 3. That all these were not struck dead in the very Fact, and upon the place, which would have terrified others from following their example; but were se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cretly struck with some Disease or Plague, which killed them in a little time. 4. That divers Learned Men translate, and understand the place otherwise, and make the number much smaller. <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> the Jew, and the Hebrew Doctors, and many others contend, that onely seventy persons were slain. Which though it seem but a small number, yet might justly be called a <ns0:hi>great slaughter,</ns0:hi> either for the quality of the persons Slain, or for the greatness and extraordinariness of the Stroke; or because it was a great Number, considering the smallness of the Place, and the sadness of the Occasion. The Words in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> are these, and thus placed, <ns0:hi>he smote of</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>among the people seventy men, fifty thousand men;</ns0:hi> where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />as, say they, The Words should have been otherwise placed, and the greater number put before the less, if this had been meant, that he smote 50 Thousand and 70 Men. And one very Learned Man renders the Words thus, <ns0:hi>He smote of the people seventy men,</ns0:hi> even <ns0:hi>fifty</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>a thousand,</ns0:hi> the Particle <ns0:hi>Mem, of,</ns0:hi> being here understood, as it is very frequently. So the meaning is, That God smote every Twentieth man of the Transgressours, as the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> used to Cut off every Tenth Man in case of the general guilt of an Army. Or the Words may be rendred thus, <ns0:hi>He smote of,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>among the people, seventy men</ns0:hi> out of <ns0:hi>fifty thousand men;</ns0:hi> the Particle <ns0:hi>Mem, of,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>out of,</ns0:hi> being understood before the Word <ns0:hi>fifty,</ns0:hi> which <ns0:hi>Bochart</ns0:hi> puts before a <ns0:hi>thousand;</ns0:hi> and it may be thus expressed, to shew, that God did temper his Severity with great Clemency: and whereas there were many thousands of Transgressors (every one following his Brothers Example, as is usual in such cases) God onely singled out 70 of the Principal Offenders, who either Sinned most against their Light, or Office; or were the Ringleaders, or Chief encou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ragers of the rest. To which may be added, That the an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cient Translators, the <ns0:hi>Syriack,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Arabick,</ns0:hi> read the Place <ns0:hi>five thousand and seventy men,</ns0:hi> being supposed to have read in their <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Copies, <ns0:hi>Chamesh, five,</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>Chamishim, fifty,</ns0:hi> which is no great alteration in the Word.</ns0:note>: and the people lamen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted, because the LORD had smitten <ns0:hi>many</ns0:hi> of the people with a great slaughter.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And the men of Bethshemesh said, Who is able to stand before <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> The Lord, this ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly God.</ns0:note> this holy LORD God <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To Minister before the Ark where the Lord is pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent. Since God is so severe to mark whatsoever is amiss in his Servants, who is sufficient and worthy to serve him? who dare presume to come into his presence? It seems to be a Complaint, or Expostulation with God, concerning this last and great instance of his Severity.</ns0:note>? and to whom shall he go up from us <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Who will dare to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive the Ark with so much hazard to themselves?</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 ¶ And they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kirjath-jearim <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Whither they sent, either because the Place was not far off from them, and so it might soon be removed, which they mainly desired: or, because it was a place of Eminency and Strength, and somewhat further distant from the <ns0:hi>Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />listines,</ns0:hi> where therefore it was likely to be better preserved from any new attempts of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> and to be better attended by the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> who would more freely and fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently come to it at such a place, than in <ns0:hi>Bethshemesh,</ns0:hi> which was upon the border of their Enemies Land: or because they thought they would gladly receive it, being a pious and zealous People: or because it was in the way to <ns0:hi>Shilo,</ns0:hi> its an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cient Habitation; and whither they might suppose it was to be carried by degrees, and several Stages, whereof this was one.</ns0:note>, saying, The Philistines have brought again the ark of the LORD: come ye down <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> fetch it up to you.</ns0:p>
